Most distributions ship programs that someone else compiled for an average computer. Lunar hands you the recipes instead. Your machine builds every program itself, from the original source code, with the options you pick, and you end up with a system that has exactly what you asked for and nothing you didn't.

One command does the whole trip. Here's what happens when you install the nano text editor:

[{"title":"Questions first","text":"Lunar asks about the options before anything compiles: colour highlighting? A .nanorc file? Multiple buffers? It asks for every dependency too, all up front, so you can walk away while it builds."},{"title":"Fetch and check","text":"Missing dependencies, like the ncurses library, get built first. Then nano's source comes straight from nano-editor.org, and Lunar checks it against the checksum in the module."},{"title":"Build","text":"The source is unpacked and compiled for your processor, with the optimization settings you chose in `lunar optimize`."},{"title":"Track","text":"As nano installs, Lunar writes down every file that lands on your system. That list is why `lrm nano` can remove it again cleanly, down to the last file."},{"title":"Liftoff","text":"nano is installed, and the compile log is kept in case you're curious how it went."}]
A module is a handful of short shell files, and you can read every one of them. Here is nano's module as it stands in November 2026, minus its long description.
says what to download and how to check it:

MODULE=nano
   VERSION=8.7.1
    SOURCE=$MODULE-$VERSION.tar.xz
SOURCE_URL=https://www.nano-editor.org/dist/v8/
SOURCE_VFY=sha256:76f0dcb248f2e2f1251d4ecd20fd30fb400a360a3a37c6c340e0a52c2d1cdedf
  WEB_SITE=https://www.nano-editor.org
   ENTERED=20010922
   UPDATED=20260326
     SHORT="Superior clone of the pico text editor"
"Superior clone of the pico text editor"

mquery COLOR  "Enable color and syntax highlighting?" y
mquery NANORC "Enable use of .nanorc file?" y
mquery MULTI  "Enable multiple file buffers?" y

compiled for your processor and your compiler flags, not for an average PC.
optional features are questions, not defaults. Say no, and they're never built.
modules are plain shell, and every build keeps a log, so when something goes wrong you can see exactly what happened.
software comes straight from the people who wrote it, patched only when necessary.

You're comfortable at a shell prompt, or you'd like to be.
You'd rather understand your system than have it guess for you.
You enjoy choosing what goes on your machine.
You don't mind waiting while big programs compile. A browser takes
about half an hour on eight cores
If that sounds like you, welcome aboard. If you'd rather never meet a compiler, there are excellent binary distributions out there, and no hard feelings.
